modules.title: Everyday fluency
modules.summary: Talk about yourself with confidence: life history, routines, personality and change.

grammar.name: Present perfect vs. past simple
grammar.explanation: Use the past simple for a finished action at a known past time, and the present perfect for experience or a situation that still matters now.
keyPoints: Past simple pairs with finished time markers: in 2019, yesterday, last summer.
Present perfect never takes a finished time marker: I have visited Lisbon three times.
Use have been (experience) rather than have gone (still away).
grammar.example: I started my first job in 2019, and I have worked in three different cities since then.

items.explanation: A finished time (2019) takes the past simple.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes life experience rather than a finished event?
options: I have visited Lisbon three times.
I was visiting Lisbon last year.
items.answer: I have visited Lisbon three times.
items.explanation: Experience with no fixed time uses the present perfect.

items.prompt: I ___ never flown alone before this trip.
items.explanation: Present perfect with 'never' describes experience up to now.

grammar.name: Narrative tenses
grammar.explanation: When you tell a story, past continuous sets the scene, past simple moves the action forward, and past perfect explains what had already happened.
keyPoints: Past continuous frames the background: I was walking home when I saw the message.
Past perfect marks the earlier of two past events: the film had already started.
Keep one main timeline; use past perfect only when the order matters.
grammar.example: I had been waiting for hours when the bus finally arrived, so I walked the last two kilometres.

items.explanation: Past perfect shows the film started before you arrived.

items.prompt: I ___ home when I saw the message.
items.explanation: Past continuous sets the background action interrupted by a shorter event.

items.prompt: We ___ for hours before the bus finally came.
items.explanation: Past perfect continuous emphasises duration before a later past moment.

inputs.title: Three people, three changes
inputs.body: LAURA: I had been teaching for six years when I finally booked a one-way ticket. I was terrified, but it turned out to be the best decision I have ever made. DIEGO: My parents came round to the idea eventually. At first they thought I was throwing away a good job, and to be honest, so did I. MARI: I only really settled down at thirty-five. Before that I was moving every eighteen months, and I had never owned furniture that I actually chose myself.

questions.prompt: How long had Laura been teaching before she booked the ticket?
How do Diego's parents feel now?
What does Mari say about her earlier life?

inputs.title: The year everything changed
inputs.body: Most people can name the year their life changed. For Ana it was 2020, when the restaurant she managed closed for good. She had spent a decade building a career she loved, and suddenly it had gone. What she remembers now is not the loss but the noise of it: one week she was planning a menu, the next she was queuing for a job she had never imagined doing. Two years later she runs a small cooking school, and she says she would not go back. The turning point, she insists, was not the closure itself but the first morning she stopped waiting for things to return to normal.

questions.prompt: What does she remember most clearly?
What does Ana identify as her real turning point?

speaking.title: Describe a major change in your life
speaking.prompt: Describe a major change in your life. What happened, how did you feel at the time, and what did you learn? Speak for 90 seconds.

speaking.title: Role-play: catching up with an old friend
speaking.prompt: You meet a friend you have not seen for five years. Ask about their life, react to their news, and share one change of your own. Two minutes.
phrases: That sounds like quite a change.
Have you kept in touch with...?

speaking.title: Shadowing: storytelling rhythm
speaking.prompt: Repeat the model story line by line, copying the stress on content words and the short pause at each thought group.
phrases: I had been living there / for about a year / when everything changed.

writing.title: Informal email: news and changes
writing.prompt: Write an informal email to a friend you have not contacted for a year. Tell them about one change in your life, ask two questions, and suggest meeting. 120–150 words.

outline.analyze: Purpose: share news and re-connect. Audience: a friend. Register: informal but correct.
outline.plan: Greeting → one clear change → two questions → suggestion → sign-off.
outline.draft: Use present perfect for news, past simple for finished details, and at least two phrasal verbs.
outline.improve: Replace 'very good' and 'nice' with precise adjectives; add one linker per paragraph.
outline.review: Check the word count, the greeting and closing, and that both questions are clear.

lessons.title: Life so far: present perfect vs. past simple
lessons.objective: Separate finished past events from life experience in a short personal history.
lessons.canDo: I can tell the story of my life so far, using the past simple for finished events and the present perfect for experience.
lessons.output: Record six sentences about your life: three finished events in the past simple and three experiences in the present perfect.

lessons.title: Listening: three people, three changes
lessons.objective: Catch time markers and attitude in short personal stories told in three accents.
lessons.canDo: I can follow a short personal story in a familiar accent and identify the speaker's attitude.
lessons.output: Retell one of the three stories in 60 seconds, keeping the timeline in order.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: personality and routines
lessons.objective: Describe character and daily habits with precise B1 collocations instead of 'nice' and 'good'.
lessons.canDo: I can describe someone's personality and daily routine using at least six topic collocations.
lessons.outputTitle: Describe a person you know well
lessons.output: Record a 60-second description of a person you know well using five of the new collocations.

lessons.title: Speaking: describing a major change
lessons.objective: Structure a 90-second account of a change with a clear beginning, middle and reflection.
lessons.canDo: I can speak for 90 seconds about a change in my life, linking ideas and reflecting at the end.
lessons.output: Use the prompt card below: what happened, how you felt, what you learned.

lessons.title: Narrative tenses: telling it properly
lessons.objective: Combine past continuous, past simple and past perfect so a story's timeline is never ambiguous.
lessons.canDo: I can tell a story with a clear timeline, using past perfect only where the order matters.
lessons.output: Tell a 90-second story about a day that went wrong, with at least one past perfect sentence.

lessons.title: Reading: the year everything changed
lessons.objective: Identify the main idea, a detail and an inferred attitude in a short narrative article.
lessons.canDo: I can read a short article about someone's life change and explain what the writer implies.
lessons.output: Write four sentences: two summarising the article and two saying whether you agree with Ana.

lessons.title: Writing: informal email about change
lessons.objective: Plan, draft and edit a 120–150-word informal email with a clear purpose and audience.
lessons.canDo: I can write an informal email of 120–150 words that shares news, asks questions and suggests a plan.
lessons.output: Write the email, then revise it once for vocabulary range and one linker per paragraph.

lessons.title: Review: module 1 consolidation
lessons.objective: Recall the module's tenses and vocabulary under light time pressure and identify your weakest area.
lessons.canDo: I can use the module's two tense systems and twelve expressions accurately in a short review task.
lessons.output: Do the practice set twice: once untimed, once in six minutes. Note every item you missed.

modules.title: Work and study
modules.summary: Careers, education and plans: talk about the future with accuracy and compare options.
modules.vocabularyTopic: Careers, education, goals and workplace communication

grammar.name: Future forms: plans, predictions, arrangements
grammar.explanation: Choose the future form by meaning: going to for intentions, will for predictions and spontaneous decisions, present continuous for fixed arrangements.
keyPoints: Fixed arrangement: I'm meeting my manager at nine tomorrow.
Intention: I'm going to apply for the internal role.
Prediction or offer: It will probably take two years. I'll send it now.
grammar.example: I'm meeting the recruiter on Thursday, and I'm going to take the online course before then; it will make the interview easier.

items.prompt: I ___ the recruiter at nine tomorrow — it is already in my calendar.
items.explanation: A fixed arrangement takes the present continuous.

options: I'm going to retrain next year.
items.answer: I'm going to retrain next year.
items.explanation: 'Going to' expresses a plan or intention rather than a promise.

items.prompt: The job ___ harder than it looks.
items.explanation: Predictions about the future use will + infinitive.

grammar.name: First and second conditionals
grammar.explanation: First conditional covers realistic future possibilities; second conditional covers imagined or unlikely present situations and polite proposals.
keyPoints: First: If I finish the course, I will ask for a promotion.
Second: If I had more time, I would study design.
Use were with I/he/she in formal second conditionals: If I were you...
grammar.example: If I pass the exam in June, I'll apply for the master's; if I had the money now, I'd already be enrolled.

items.prompt: If I ___ the exam in June, I will apply for the master's.
items.explanation: The first conditional uses the present simple in the if-clause.

items.prompt: If I had more time, I ___ a second language.
items.explanation: Imagined present situations take would + infinitive.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the most diplomatic way to give advice?
options: If I am you, I apply.
If I were you, I would negotiate the salary.
If I was you, I will negotiate.
items.answer: If I were you, I would negotiate the salary.
items.explanation: 'If I were you, I would...' is the standard diplomatic formula.

inputs.title: A careers podcast: two routes
inputs.body: HOST: So, Priya, you left banking at thirty-two. PRIYA: I did, and everyone thought I had lost my mind. I had a good salary, but I was going to burn out, I could feel it. The plan was to take six months off and then retrain as a data analyst. HOST: And it worked? PRIYA: Mostly. The studying was harder than the job had been, but I get far more job satisfaction now. If I were starting again, I would save more money first, though.

questions.prompt: How old was Priya when she left banking?
What would she change if she started again?
options: She would save more money first
questions.answer: She would save more money first

inputs.title: Is a degree still worth it?
inputs.body: For decades the advice was simple: go to university, get a degree, get ahead. That advice still holds for many careers, especially medicine and law, but it is no longer automatic. Employers increasingly ask what a candidate can do rather than where they studied. Short-term contracts, portfolio careers and mid-career retraining have made the single, linear career path much rarer. None of this means a degree is wasted. It means the return depends on the subject, the country and, above all, what the student does with the three years beyond attending lectures.

questions.prompt: What is the article's main point?
options: A degree is no longer automatically worth it
questions.answer: A degree is no longer automatically worth it

questions.prompt: Which factor does the writer highlight above all?
options: What the student does beyond lectures
questions.answer: What the student does beyond lectures

speaking.title: Compare two career paths
speaking.prompt: Compare two career paths you know well. Which would you choose, and why? Speak for two minutes.

speaking.title: Role-play: the job interview
speaking.prompt: You are interviewing for a role you are slightly under-qualified for. Answer three questions about your plans, your weaknesses and why you want the job. Two minutes.
phrases: One thing I'm working on is...

speaking.title: Shadowing: future forms in fast speech
speaking.prompt: Shadow the clip twice, paying attention to how going to is reduced to gonna and how will merges with the subject.
phrases: I'm going to apply / as soon as I finish the course.
It'll probably take / about six months.

writing.title: Opinion paragraph: work and study
writing.prompt: Write a 150-word opinion paragraph answering: is a university degree still the best route to a good career? Give a clear position and two reasons.

outline.analyze: Purpose: argue a position. Audience: an educated general reader. Format: one paragraph or two short ones.
outline.plan: Position in the first sentence → reason one with an example → reason two → concession → restated position.
outline.draft: Use one first or second conditional and two future forms.
outline.improve: Vary sentence openings; replace 'a lot of' with a precise quantifier.
outline.review: Check the position is visible in the first and last sentences.

lessons.title: Future forms: plans, predictions, arrangements
lessons.objective: Choose between going to, will and the present continuous according to meaning, not habit.
lessons.canDo: I can talk about my plans, arrangements and predictions using the right future form.
lessons.output: Record 60 seconds on your plans for the next year: three arrangements and two predictions.

lessons.title: Listening: a careers podcast
lessons.objective: Extract dates, reasons and hypothetical regrets from a two-speaker interview.
lessons.canDo: I can follow an interview about a career change and note the reasons behind the decision.
lessons.output: Take notes under three headings — decision, difficulty, advice — then summarise in three sentences.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: careers and the workplace
lessons.objective: Use twelve workplace collocations accurately in speech and writing.
lessons.canDo: I can describe a job, its pressures and its rewards using precise workplace vocabulary.
lessons.output: Record 60 seconds describing your job or course with six of the new expressions.

lessons.title: Speaking: comparing two career paths
lessons.objective: Compare options fairly and reach a justified conclusion in two minutes.
lessons.canDo: I can compare two options, weigh them up and justify a choice with linking language.
lessons.output: Use the prompt card: compare, weigh up, decide.

lessons.title: First conditional: realistic futures
lessons.objective: Build first-conditional sentences for realistic possibilities and consequences.
lessons.canDo: I can talk about realistic future possibilities and their consequences.
lessons.output: Record six first-conditional sentences about your studies or work.

lessons.title: Second conditional: imagined options
lessons.objective: Use the second conditional for imaginary situations and diplomatic advice.
lessons.canDo: I can discuss imagined situations and give diplomatic advice with the second conditional.
lessons.outputTitle: If I could change one thing
lessons.output: Speak for 60 seconds: if you could change one thing about your working life, what would it be?

lessons.title: Reading: is a degree still worth it?
lessons.objective: Identify the writer's argument, a concession and the key supporting factor.

lessons.output: Write the main claim, one concession and your own view in five sentences.

lessons.title: Writing: opinion paragraph
lessons.objective: State and support a position in 150 words with a clear structure.
lessons.canDo: I can write a 150-word opinion paragraph with a clear position and two supported reasons.
